Conflagration

kon-fluh-GRAY-shun -- from Latin conflagrare ('to burn up'), from com- (intensive) + flagrare ('to blaze'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Conflagration is an extensive, destructive fire that consumes a large area of land or property.

A cigarette carelessly discarded behind the print shop sparked a conflagration that gutted three city blocks before dawn.

Worked Example

Investigators later determined that a faulty generator, left running overnight in the storage room, had sparked the conflagration that destroyed all six warehouses.

That scale -- a small spark growing into a fire that swallows an entire block of buildings -- is exactly what conflagration describes, not just any ordinary house fire.

How Strong Is It? — blaze → conflagration → inferno

blaze vs. conflagration

blaze vs. conflagration: A blaze broke out in the kitchen but was put out with a fire extinguisher before it could spread.

inferno vs. conflagration

inferno vs. conflagration: Inferno is more extreme than conflagration: a conflagration devours whole blocks of buildings, but an inferno — like the stairwell the trapped firefighters described — is fire at its fiercest, an inescapable furnace.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together, intensifying (Latin com-, which takes the form con- before f)

Root — flagr-

Root — flagr-: to blaze, burn (Latin flagrare)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: action or result of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Conflagration comes from Latin com- (intensifying 'together,' appearing here as con-) plus flagrare ('to blaze'): con- + flagr- + -ation -- so a conflagration is, at its root, an intensely blazing fire, everything burning together at once.

Use the root in a new word: deflagration

Use the root in a new word: deflagration: Engineers studied the sudden deflagration inside the engine to figure out what had gone wrong.

Root Check

Word Choice

Conflagration is a formal, almost literary word -- reserve it for fires large enough to threaten whole buildings, blocks, or landscapes, not a candle or a campfire.
